newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy slowed in the spring, price rises muted.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy slowed in the spring, price rises muted.

text.p: Consumers cut their spending in the spring, sharply curtailing the economy's second-quarter growth as prices rose at the slowest rate since the 1960s, the Commerce Department said Thursday.

Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of total U.S. economic activity, expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the April-June second quarter, less than half the revised 4.9 percent pace in the first quarter.

Analysts said the slowdown in GDP growth, coupled with a virtual absence of inflation, was heartening because it meant the Federal Reserve was under little or no pressure to raise interest rates soon.

"The economy continues to look very healthy -- the best it has looked in decades, if not ever," said economist Allen Sinai of Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston. "There is nothing in this report to disturb the Fed."
A key inflation measure in the GDP report -- the implicit price deflator -- edged up at only a 1.4 percent rate in the second quarter after a 2.4 percent first-quarter increase.

It was the slowest rate of quarterly price rises since a 0.9 percent gain in the second quarter of 1964. The figures were even more striking because the economy is now in its seventh year of unbroken growth since the last recession ended in March 1991.

Clinton administration officials hailed the GDP report as a sign the economy was set to continue its winning ways, which have brought strong job and income growth and a flood of tax revenues to whittle down the government's budget deficit.

"The economy continues to hum: growth is robust, unemployment remains low at 5 percent, inflation is in check, household wealth is rising and consumer confidence surveys register record optimism," said White House Economic Adviser Janet Yellen after a meeting with President Clinton to discuss the report.

"We're in a period of strong, stable economic expansion," said Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers. Lee Price, the Commerce Department's acting undersecretary for economic affairs, said second-quarter GDP appeared likely to expand at around a 2.5 percent annual rate.

The Commerce Department previously reported that GDP shot ahead at a 5.9 percent annual rate in the first quarter. It trimmed that estimate back to 4.9 percent as part of a broader set of revisions to the national income and production accounts, beginning with the first quarter of 1993.

Revisions are made each July to incorporate more complete and accurate data from sources, in this case including updated federal government budget information as well as price changes for semiconductors and computers, which have grown steadily cheaper and helped keep inflation in check.

The Federal Reserve last raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in March and has held them steady at two subsequent meetings of its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee. It is next scheduled to meet Aug. 19.

Growth in consumer spending braked abruptly in the second quarter to a $9.8 billion annual rate from $61.7 billion in the first quarter -- the key reason for the second-quarter slowdown, because spending on goods and services fuels two-thirds of national economic activity.

Businesses added to their inventories at a $66.8 billion annual rate in the second quarter. That was about the same as the very strong $63.7 billion addition to inventories they made in the first quarter, when stocks were being built up at a much more rapid rate than late in 1996.

Some analysts cautioned the second-quarter slowdown in the economy may be temporary and that growth could snap back quickly. Consumers have rising incomes from plentiful jobs and from stock market gains, a capital spending boom is under way and exports are relatively brisk.

"The real issue is that at some point, given the strength I think will soon reappear in demand, will that trigger a change in inflation psychology that will make it harder to keep prices in check," said economist Dick Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
Berner said it was possible that GDP could reaccelerate to an annual rate of growth around 4 percent in the third quarter.

A separate report from the Purchasing Management Association of Chicago showed its July index falling to 60.6 from 61.5 in June as orders and production eased. But prices paid by manufacturers in the Midwest picked up in July.
Labour markets also remain very tight, which analysts caution can bring pressure for higher wages, though big increases have not yet shown up.

The Labour Department said first-time jobless claims plunged to 277,000 last week from 299,000 the week before. The four-week moving average that smoothes out week-to-week swings slipped to 325,750 from 340,750.

Also on Thursday, the Conference Board said its help-wanted advertising index rose 7 points in June to 88.0 vs. an 81.0 reading in May. The index stood at 85.0 a year ago. The Conference Board surveys help-wanted advertising volume in 51 major newspapers across the country every month.
